metadata.title: Image Histogram - View RGB & Brightness Distribution Online
metadata.description: Free online image histogram viewer: RGB channels and brightness distribution at a glance. Processed entirely in your browser.

image-histogram.title: Image Histogram
image-histogram.description: View the RGB channel and brightness histogram of your image to understand its exposure and color distribution. All analysis happens locally in your browser — your image is never uploaded.

faqs.question: What is an image histogram?
faqs.answer: A histogram counts how many pixels sit at each brightness level (0-255): the horizontal axis is brightness and the vertical axis is pixel count. It gives you an instant read on your image's exposure and contrast.

faqs.question: How can I tell if my image is overexposed or underexposed?
faqs.answer: If the histogram bunches up on the right side (near 255), the image is overexposed; if it bunches up on the left (near 0), it's underexposed. A well-exposed image usually has a fairly even spread.

faqs.question: What's the difference between an RGB histogram and a brightness histogram?
faqs.answer: An RGB histogram charts the red, green, and blue channels separately, while a brightness histogram combines them by how bright they appear to the human eye — making it better for judging overall exposure.

faqs.question: Is my image uploaded anywhere?
faqs.answer: No. All analysis happens locally in your browser — your image never leaves your device.

whatIs.title: What Is an Image Histogram?
body: An image histogram charts how many pixels sit at each brightness level (0-255). The horizontal axis is brightness — dark on the left, bright on the right — and the vertical axis is the number of pixels at that brightness.

By reading the histogram you can quickly tell whether an image is properly exposed, whether its contrast is high or low, and whether the colors are shifted. It's one of the most common diagnostic tools in photography and design.

howTo.title: How to View an Image Histogram
howTo.intro: Three steps to view your image histogram:
items: Click the upload area and choose a local image (PNG, JPG, WEBP, or BMP supported).
The histogram is generated automatically as soon as the image loads.
Switch between RGB channels and brightness modes to inspect different dimensions of the color distribution.

tips.title: Tips
items: If the histogram leans left, the image is dark; if it leans right, the image is bright.
In RGB mode, the overlap of the three channels indicates color balance — a strong shift toward one channel means a color cast.
If the histogram is pushed against both edges with a hollow middle, the image has very high contrast.

faqs.question: How does color extraction work?
faqs.answer: The tool uses a median cut algorithm to analyze every pixel, group similar colors together, and average each group into one representative color — giving you the color combination that best represents the image.

faqs.question: Is more colors always better?
faqs.answer: Not necessarily. 4-8 colors are usually enough to capture an image's overall tone. More colors add more detail but can also produce near-duplicate shades, so pick based on the image's complexity.

faqs.question: What format are the extracted colors in?
faqs.answer: Every swatch shows its HEX value (e.g. #FF5733). Click a swatch to copy it in one click, ready to paste into your design tool.

metadata.title: Image Perceptual Hash - Compute pHash Online
metadata.description: Free online tool to compute the perceptual hash (pHash) of an image. The 64-bit hash is ideal for similar-image comparison and deduplication.

image-phash.title: Image Perceptual Hash (pHash)
image-phash.description: Compute the perceptual hash (pHash) of an image. pHash compresses image content into a 64-bit fingerprint, and similar images produce similar hashes — ideal for duplicate detection and similarity comparison.

faqs.question: What is a perceptual hash (pHash)?
faqs.answer: A perceptual hash is a content-aware image fingerprint: the image is shrunk and converted to grayscale, DCT is applied to extract low-frequency features, and a 64-bit hash is produced. Similar images get similar hashes.

faqs.question: How is pHash different from a regular hash?
faqs.answer: Regular hashes like MD5 or SHA are extremely sensitive — changing a single pixel changes the result completely. pHash focuses on the image's overall structure, so recompression, resizing, or slight color tweaks barely affect it.

faqs.question: How do I use the hash to tell if two images are similar?
faqs.answer: Compute the Hamming distance between the two hashes (the number of differing bits). The smaller the distance, the more similar — generally under 10-12 bits means highly similar.

faqs.question: Is my image uploaded anywhere?
faqs.answer: No. All computation happens locally in your browser — your image never leaves your device.

whatIs.title: What Is a Perceptual Hash?
body: A perceptual hash squeezes an image into a fixed-length fingerprint (64 bits here) while ensuring that visually similar images get similar fingerprints.
It works by extracting low-frequency features in the frequency domain with DCT, ignoring compression, resizing, and slight color shifts that don't affect how we perceive the image.

howTo.title: How to Compute an Image Perceptual Hash
howTo.intro: Three steps to compute the pHash of your image:
items: Upload a local image (PNG, JPG, WEBP, or BMP supported).
Click Compute Hash to generate the 64-bit hash value.
Copy the HEX or binary result for programmatic comparison or archiving.

tips.title: Tips
items: Different compression or resized versions of the same image produce nearly identical hashes.
A Hamming distance under 10-12 bits indicates similar images.
Pair this tool with Duplicate Image Finder to deduplicate images in bulk.

image-compare.title: Image Compare
image-compare.description: Upload two images, compare them pixel by pixel, and get a difference ratio plus a red-highlighted difference map — a quick way to pinpoint exactly what changed.

faqs.question: How is the difference ratio calculated?
faqs.answer: The second image is resized to match the first, then the two are compared pixel by pixel. Pixels whose color difference exceeds a threshold are counted as different, and their share of the total is the difference ratio.

faqs.question: What does red mean in the difference map?
faqs.answer: Red highlights mark the areas where the two images differ. Everything else is dimmed so you can spot every difference at a glance.

faqs.question: Can I compare images of different sizes?
faqs.answer: Yes. The tool automatically resizes the second image to match the first before comparing pixel by pixel.

metadata.title: Duplicate Image Finder - Batch Detect Similar Images Online

duplicate-finder.title: Duplicate Image Finder
duplicate-finder.description: Upload multiple images at once. Each image gets a perceptual hash, and duplicates or highly similar images are grouped automatically — perfect for reclaiming disk space.

faqs.question: How are duplicate images detected?
faqs.answer: Every image is hashed with a perceptual hash (pHash). Images whose Hamming distance is small enough (similar enough) are automatically grouped together.

faqs.question: Can it detect modified images?
faqs.answer: Yes. Perceptual hashes are insensitive to resizing, compression, and slight color adjustments, so recompressed or resized copies are recognized too.

faqs.question: How many images can I upload at once?
faqs.answer: Up to 20 images at a time. Need to check more? Just run the detection in batches.

faqs.question: Is my image uploaded anywhere?
faqs.answer: No. All detection happens locally in your browser — your images never leave your device.

whatIs.title: What Is Duplicate Image Detection?
body: Duplicate image detection generates a perceptual hash fingerprint for every image, compares the fingerprints pairwise with Hamming distance, and groups highly similar images together.
It's far more reliable than comparing file sizes or names — even copies with different names or dimensions are caught as long as the content matches.

howTo.title: How to Find Duplicate Images

Images in the same group may not be pixel-identical — preview before deleting.
Great for cleaning up downloaded assets, photo backups, and other duplicated content.

faqs.question: What is an RGB channel?
faqs.answer: An RGB image is made of red, green, and blue color channels layered together. Each channel records the brightness of its own color, and the three combined produce the final displayed color.

faqs.question: What do the separated channel images look like?
faqs.answer: The red channel image keeps only red brightness information (the picture appears in red tones), and the green and blue channels work the same way. The brighter a channel, the stronger that color is in that area.

faqs.question: What is channel splitting used for?
faqs.answer: It's commonly used to learn color theory, create channel assets, diagnose color casts, and for color separation in professional print workflows.

image-to-ascii.description: Convert an image into ASCII art made of characters, with an adjustable output width and an invert mode. Copy the result to your clipboard or download it as a text file.

faqs.question: What is ASCII art?
faqs.answer: ASCII art uses the density of different characters to mimic the brightness of an image — denser characters represent darker areas and sparser characters represent brighter ones.

faqs.question: What does the width setting do?
faqs.answer: The width (number of columns) determines how many characters the output uses. More columns mean more detail but a wider result; fewer columns produce a more abstract look.

faqs.question: What does invert mean?
faqs.answer: Invert flips the brightness mapping, using sparse characters for dark areas and dense characters for bright ones — useful for displaying on dark backgrounds.

faqs.question: Can I save the result?
faqs.answer: Yes. You can copy it to your clipboard with one click, or download it as a .txt file.

faqs.answer: A sprite combines several small images into one larger image. CSS background-position is used to show just one part of it, reducing HTTP requests and speeding up loading.

faqs.question: What's the difference between the three layouts?
faqs.answer: The horizontal layout arranges all images side by side, the vertical layout stacks them vertically, and the grid layout arranges them into rows and columns of roughly square cells.

faqs.question: How do I use the generated CSS?

faqs.question: What's the difference between Blob URL and DataURL?
faqs.answer: A Blob URL (starting with blob:) points to an object in the browser's memory and is great for in-page use. A DataURL is a Base64-encoded string that can be embedded directly into HTML/CSS, making it easy to share and store.

faqs.question: Can a Blob URL be used long term?
faqs.answer: No. A Blob URL is only valid within the current page session and becomes invalid after a refresh or when the page is closed.

faqs.question: Are there any downsides to DataURL?
faqs.answer: Base64 encoding increases the size by about 33% and is not ideal for large images, but it's convenient for embedding directly in code.

faqs.question: Is my image uploaded to a server?
faqs.answer: No. The conversion happens entirely locally in your browser.

image-similarity.title: Image Similarity
image-similarity.description: Upload two images to calculate pixel-level similarity, mean squared error (MSE), and peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR), with an adjustable tolerance threshold.

faqs.question: How is similarity calculated?
faqs.answer: The RGB values are compared pixel by pixel. Two pixels are considered similar when their color difference is within the tolerance, and the similarity percentage is the proportion of similar pixels.

faqs.question: What do MSE and PSNR mean?
faqs.answer: MSE (mean squared error) is smaller when the two images are closer. PSNR (peak signal-to-noise ratio) is measured in dB — above 30 dB generally indicates near-lossless quality.

faqs.question: What happens if I increase the tolerance?
faqs.answer: A larger tolerance treats pixels with small color differences as similar, so similarity increases. A smaller tolerance makes the comparison stricter.

faqs.question: Can images of different sizes be compared?
faqs.answer: Yes. The tool scales both images to the same size before comparing them pixel by pixel.

faqs.question: What is the difference between animated WebP and GIF?
faqs.answer: At the same visual quality, an animated WebP is usually only 30%-50% of a GIF's size, supports 16 million colors, and compresses better — though some older platforms don't support it.

faqs.question: What is the difference between lossless and lossy?
faqs.answer: Lossless compression keeps full quality but produces larger files; lossy compression slightly reduces quality for much smaller files, which suits photo-like content.

faqs.question: Will the generated WebP loop automatically?
faqs.answer: Yes. The converted animated WebP loops infinitely by default.

faqs.question: How long does the conversion take?
faqs.answer: The first run downloads the ~30MB FFmpeg engine (cached afterwards); then conversion speed depends on the video's length and resolution.

video-thumbnail.title: Video Thumbnail
video-thumbnail.description: Automatically capture multiple frames from a video and combine them into a single thumbnail grid (contact sheet), with customizable rows, columns, thumbnail width, and optional per-frame timestamps.

faqs.question: What is a thumbnail grid?
faqs.answer: A thumbnail grid (contact sheet) arranges multiple frames of a video into rows and columns on a single image, so you can quickly overview the video's content.

faqs.question: How are the frames selected?
faqs.answer: Frames are distributed evenly across the whole video. For example, 3 rows × 4 columns gives 12 frames captured at equal intervals from start to finish.

faqs.question: Can timestamps be displayed?
faqs.answer: Yes. When Show Timestamps is enabled, each frame is labeled with its time position (minutes:seconds) in the video.

faqs.question: What format is the generated image?
faqs.answer: The output is a PNG image whose dimensions depend on the rows, columns, and thumbnail width. Download it for use as a video cover or index page.

video-to-images.title: Video to Images
video-to-images.description: Extract frames from a video at fixed time intervals and save them as PNG, JPEG, WebP, BMP, or TIFF. Powered by FFmpeg WebAssembly, it supports 20+ video container formats including MKV, AVI, FLV, and TS, all processed locally in your browser.

faqs.question: Which video formats are supported?
faqs.answer: Based on FFmpeg decoding, it supports 20+ container formats including MP4, MKV, AVI, MOV, FLV, WebM, M2TS, TS, OGV, MXF, 3GP, WMV, and VOB.

faqs.question: Which image formats can I export?
faqs.answer: Five formats are supported: PNG, JPEG, WebP, BMP, and TIFF. PNG is lossless and great for assets; JPEG is smaller for quick previews.

faqs.question: How do I set the extraction interval?
faqs.answer: The interval is how many seconds between each extracted frame. Smaller intervals give more frames for smoother coverage; larger intervals use less storage. To protect memory, a maximum of 150 frames can be extracted at once.

faqs.question: Are videos uploaded to a server?
faqs.answer: No. Videos are decoded locally in your browser with FFmpeg WebAssembly and never leave your device. First use downloads an ~30MB engine (cached afterwards).

faqs.question: What is a long image?
faqs.answer: A long image stitches every page of a PDF vertically into one complete picture for continuous reading, ideal for sharing on social platforms or archiving.

faqs.question: How do I choose the sharpness?
faqs.answer: Sharpness is the render scale: 1x is smallest, 3x is sharpest. Very large images may hit browser canvas limits; lower the scale in that case.

faqs.question: PNG or JPEG?
faqs.answer: PNG is lossless with crisp text but larger; JPEG is smaller and suits big documents. Use JPEG for regular documents and PNG for documents with screenshots.

faqs.question: Is the document uploaded to a server?
faqs.answer: No. The PDF is rendered and merged locally with pdf.js in your browser and never leaves your device.

faqs.question: How many images can I stitch?
faqs.answer: Up to 20 images. You can reorder or remove any image in the list and re-stitch.

faqs.question: How are images with different sizes handled?
faqs.answer: Center mode keeps each image's original aspect ratio centered; stretch mode stretches images to the alignment width (vertical) or height (horizontal).

faqs.question: How do I use a transparent background?

faqs.question: The result is too large. What can I do?
